utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case IT-04-81-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Mark Harmon and Faith Devine for the Prosecution. My case manager, Carmela Javier, is also appearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Jim Castle and Novak Lukic appearing on behalf of Momcilo Perisic, who is not present. Also with us today is case manager, Tina Drolec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Castle. I begin this Status Conference by looking first at the pending motions. There is a motion from the Defence for the appointment of an amicus counsel to report to the Chamber on equality of arms. And I have to say that a decision will be given shortly on this motion. There is the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts relating to Sarajevo. Mr. Harmon, I have personally dealt with two motions for adjudicated facts, but as a Judge of a Trial Chamber, and I would hate to have, as a Judge of a Trial Chamber, a Pre-Trial Judge dealing with this matter. In my view, it is much better to have it dealt with by the Trial Chamber. I'm going to leave this motion for the Trial Chamber, but it will not affect the Prosecution's duty to file its witness list. Then there is an application for an order pursuant to Rule 54 bis, directing the government of the Republic of Serbia to comply with outstanding requests for assistance. The Chamber had, on the 18th of April, issued an order inviting the Republic of Serbia to file a report on the outstanding requests for assistance by the 21st of May, and I have that report at hand. Do you have it, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we are scheduled to file a response to that report on the 29th, which we will do in due course and it will be an exhaustive report analysing precisely what we say is non-compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It will analyse what we will assert in our filing to be non-compliance with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll await that. I believe you're referring to paragraph 4 and when I have your reply, then the Chamber will decide what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is also a Defence motion for extension of time to file responses to the Prosecution's motions for the introduction of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, ter and quater, and 89. In view of the large number of 92 bis statements to be reviewed by the Defence, I will give the Defence an additional four weeks to respond, which means that the deadline for the response will be Tuesday, the 19th of June, 2007. Next are disclosure matters, Rule 66(A)(i), supporting material to the indictment; 66(A)(ii), Witness statements; 68, exculpatory material; 66(B) and 94 bis, expert reports. I understand that there are no issues relating to these matters. The length of the trial may be a little difficult for you, Mr. Harmon, but what would be your best estimate at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's very difficult, Your Honour, simply because without a decision on the 92 bis motions and the adjudicated facts, it's merely a guess, and I would be very, very reluctant, Your Honour, to even furnish that at this point in time. I think it would take, worst case scenario -- I can try to give you some guidance, but worst case scenario, if none of the 92 bis motions are granted, it would seem to me that the trial will last, assuming there is a sitting of five days a week in the normal course of business with very few interruptions, I would think it would last a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if 90 per cent of the 92 bis motions are granted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that -- certainly, it would be reduced. I can't say how much. I would want to go back and give you a better answer than a guess. We also have adjudicated facts which are before the Court, which could resolve and shorten considerably the amount of evidence that we would lead in the case. It may be, in fact, Your Honour, that if the adjudicated facts motions are granted, some of them relate directly to scheduled incidents that are in the schedules relating to the sniping and the shelling of Sarajevo. If those aspects of the adjudicated facts motions were to be granted, I certainly think that would put us in a position of possibly not having to call those witnesses at all, which would again reduce the scope and length of the trial, but I'm hard pressed to give you any guidance in the absence of those two considerable sets of motions that directly impact on how much evidence we need to prepare and present to a court viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate the effort that you have made. The trial date, it's not possible for me to say when the trial will begin, but Mr. Castle, I understand that there is a matter that you would wish to be taken into consideration. If you don't wish to mention it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No, no. The only -- the Defence has -- isn't located here and we have to move here relatively quickly when a trial date is set. My understanding is that the trial could be as early as September, most likely in October, but it could be as far as January. I'm not alone, and I have a family to move, along with me, and schools and things of that nature and to the extent that the Trial Chamber that is assigned this case can give us advance notice, I would request it. We also have -- it's not just myself but also other -- we have to assemble Defence team members for the case and have them move to Holland also, and the logistics of that is -- it's pretty onerous. So to the extent that we can get advance notice we are asking for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I understand, your entire family would move.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I take note of it and I say so so that it can be placed on the record so that the extent that it can be taken into account, it will. Mr. Castle, in your pre-trial brief, at paragraph 140, you had requested the Prosecution to file a reply opening brief, and the basis for this request, as I understand, is that it would shorten the length of the trial, as the Prosecution's reply would disclose whether it, the Prosecution, is contesting certain factual and legal issues raised by the Defence. I understand this matter was raised at the 65 ter conference, and are you still maintaining that position? Because if you are, then I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. We believe that the whole purpose of the pre-trial briefs is to narrow the issues down so that the fact finder can focus in on what is in dispute and what is not. The Prosecution's brief dealing with the two legal theories here, one being command responsibility, the other being complicity, i.e. aiding and abetting, their brief essentially merely discussed the state of the law as it's been applied in intrastate cases, and this particular case is a different animal. It's a different kind of case. It's one that where the Prosecution is asking to break some very new ground, and I believe that-- we've tried to address that fairly extensively in our brief. We believe that it helps everyone, not just the Trial Chamber, but the parties, to know where it is the Prosecution is coming in on this -- on these issues. Additionally, after, literally I think it was 72 hours after they filed their brief, the decision, the ICJ decision on BiH versus Serbia came down. That decision addressed a number of factual and legal issues that are addressed in our case. Now, granted it's not binding precedent upon the ICTY but it is persuasive, and I think it would be beneficial to all of us to know to the extent to which the Prosecution is asserting that the legal standard is different than what is -- was being set forth in the ICJ decision, and what they dispute factually from that so that we know -- it will tell us many things. It will tell us how long this trial is going to be, where the focus of our efforts need to be placed, and frankly I just don't see that there's any downside to us having this additional information. I'm not asking him to do a full brief on all the issues, just the limited ones that we set forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what's your position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our position is first of all in respect of the ICJ judgement, it's not a precedent. The ICJ case dealt with different legal issues. It had different factual evidence before it. As I said at the 65 ter conference, our evidence will be substantially more robust than the evidence that was available to the ICJ in -- when it rendered its decision, so I think clearly the clarifying and making distinctions on a judgement that has no precedential value is not the best use of the Prosecution's time. Second of all, I believe, Your Honour, that if the Trial Chamber that would be assigned to this case wants additional guidance as to the law, it would be the appropriate Chamber to request briefing on the matter but at this point in time, in my opinion, Your Honour, that is not necessary. We have set out the law and the Defence has set out its version of the law, and I think it's now incumbent on a Trial Chamber to review the matter and decide if it wants additional briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the first two matters that are mentioned in I think it's paragraph 141, the -- that the Prosecution would identify the matters with which the Prosecutor takes issue in the accused's pre-trial brief and in the case of each such matter the reason why the Prosecutor takes issue with it? Forgetting for the moment the ICJ decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that it's certainly possible to identify those matters where we take issue, but in terms of a full briefing, as to why we take issue with those matters, I don't think that that would be a useful effort on our part because the Trial Chamber may well have its own views, it may well be satisfied with the exposition of the law and it may not require that. Second of all, insofar as the factual issues where we take -- where there are differences, that's a matter for the trial, and we intend to put forth our case, not respond to the Defence's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In 65 ter (F), the Defence is required to state the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, and 3, in the case of each such matter the reason why the accused takes issue with it. So I understand Mr. Castle is asking the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is -- he may be asking -- he is asking the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But there is no provision in the rules, first of all, and I don't want to hide behind a technical argument, but there's no provision in the rules that at this point the Prosecution has to reply. Otherwise there will be endless sets of briefing back and forth. I think that this -- the purpose of Rule 65 was to identify the issues. Where are the differences? We've -- this exercise of the Prosecution pre-trial brief and the Defence pre-trial brief has now succeeded in accomplishing that. It's identified the issues where there are disputes. Now asking the Prosecution at this stage to brief again and set forth why we take -- explain why we have issues, I think, is one, as I say, not required by the rules and, two, I think best left to a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any precedent for this, Mr. Castle, in the trial -- in the Tribunal's case law?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: No. I found no precedents. It has not been argued by either side, but I think perhaps the reason for that is most Defence teams do not put forth a very explicit opening brief, and therefore, I think they are not in the position where they could ask in fairness for this type of knowledge. I just don't want to be spending a lot of time proving facts that we set forth in our brief that they are not disputing. No more than they wish to do so. And so far, throughout this whole process, it's been a process where the Defence has had to identify which of the Prosecution's facts it disputes and which ones it doesn't so that we can assist them in narrowing down their case. All we are asking for is a quid pro quo with respect to those factual assertions that we put forth in our case, in our brief, and I think that other than fundamental fairness, there is no set -- there is nothing in the rules which require it, but it would seem that everything -- when you read the entire rules in total, what they set forth is a desire that only the disputed facts in a case be presented for efficiency reasons, if for no other reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. What I will do is -- you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Castle and I have a history of being able to resolve some of our factual disputes by agreement and we will be filing with the Court a set -- a pleading setting forth where we have factual agreements. This is precisely the kind of an exercise that we can embark on over the remaining months to try to narrow the issues ourselves. We may agree, we may disagree, but I think Mr. Castle and I will be in a position to pretty much narrow the exercise. I think it's also a process -- Mr. Castle is from the United States. Because he's not here often, we don't have that much of an opportunity to get together and sit down and talk through these issues. We will have those opportunities, I think, in the future, and what Mr. Castle has asked for, in other words, to try to identify what facts are not -- that he's set forth that aren't in dispute, we can resolve those without additional pleadings, Your Honour. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Castle, you would be content with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Well, I'd prefer to see it in writing, in the manner which we had to. It wasn't a very detailed portion of our brief. Literally I think it was about seven or eight pages, we went through the factual assertions and said why we disagreed with them, literally in a two or three-sentence format. I would prefer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I would say is that the parties should work on this issue and if there is no resolution, then Mr. Castle can resurrect the matter. I would be prepared to treat it as a motion. But in the meantime the parties will work on a resolution of this matter. As I indicated before, the exhibit list of the Prosecution is to be filed, notwithstanding the decision that I have made that the motion for adjudicated facts is to be determined by the Trial Chamber, and the date for this filing will be four weeks' time, Wednesday, the 20th of June. Now, Mr. Harmon, there are some matters relating to protective measures, three witnesses, MP 003, MP 004 and MP 0014, and on the 16th of November, the Trial Chamber had ordered the Prosecution to disclose the unredacted statements of these witnesses by no later than 30 days before the commencement of trial, and the Prosecution was also ordered to disclose the identities and the unredacted witness statements of the Rule 70 witnesses in Annex B by no later than the 2nd of February, 2007, or remove the witnesses from the witness list. Mr. Harmon, is there any reason why the Chamber should not now remove these witnesses from the witness list, since, as I understand it, there has been no compliance?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of MP 003, MP 004 and MP 014, and the order of the 16th of November, we have complied with that order of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the other matter, the identities and the unredacted witness statements of the Rule 70 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Rule 70 witnesses, we have complied with as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was that done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My information is that there has not been compliance, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am informed that in respect of MP 003, MP 004 and MP 0014 that we were ordered by the Trial Chamber to disclose the unredacted statements of these witnesses no later than 30 days before the commencement of the trial. Since we don't have a trial date thus far, we have not been in a position to disclose the unredacted statements of those witnesses. In respect of the Rule 70 witnesses, we were instructed to disclose the identities and unredacted statements of those witnesses no later than the 2nd of February or remove witnesses from the witness list, and I'm informed that we have complied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What have you done? You have disclosed or you have removed them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've done both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, you have disclosed some, and those that you have not disclosed, you have removed? Well, can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you direct the Chamber, direct me, then, to the relevant document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have that information at hand. I'm certainly in a position after this to collect that information and provide it to the Senior Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because he tells me that there has been no compliance. What I'll do then is, you will provide that information to the Senior Legal Officer after we adjourn, and if you are unable to because you haven't complied, then the Chamber will issue an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I will -- the representations I have made to you are based on the information that's available to me. I will be confirming that. I will have a conversation directly with the legal officer. But it's also my independent recollection that that has been complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the matter will then proceed on the basis that I just identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, there are another class of witnesses that are of concern. After the Court's order from October, the Prosecution filed its Rule 65 ter list and summary in I believe March. When we received that, there were a number of additional protected witnesses. They are denominated MP 1 and 2, MP 5 all the way to MP 13 and then MP 15, 16 and 17. So essentially there's 14 new protected witnesses. Now, Defence has not been informed of any orders from any Chambers that protect these witnesses. We haven't been informed of whether a petition has been sought of Your Honour. My understanding is is that these are witnesses who may have been subject to protective orders in other cases. The Defence, under Rule 75, has the right to object to the terms of -- the protective terms of these witnesses. We don't know what those are. In reading through the case law, there is a number of different ways Chambers have dealt with protected witnesses. In many instances, for example, the Defence is provided with the statements and have the names redacted using an anonymous name of some sort. We don't know the terms of any of these witnesses, and so it's our understanding of the rules that the Prosecution's required to notify us not only of the Chamber in which the protective order was issued but the terms of that protective order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what can you say about these witnesses, MP 001, 2, 5, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17? What is their status?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell the situation is not as dire as was presented in the 65 ter conference. In respect of MP 16 and MP 17, both the names and the transcripts of those witnesses, transcript of statements of those witnesses, was disclosed to the Defence on the 2nd of February 2007. In respect of MP 001, MP 002 and MP 008, redacted statements of those -- a redacted statement from each of those witnesses was disclosed to the Defence in the confirming material. I am in the process of reviewing the other matters. I know there are some -- in some cases some very severe protective orders that relate to the others. I'm in the process of reviewing those. I will make decisions on those and to the extent that additional materials can be disclosed to the Defence that are consistent with the previous court orders and the rule, Rule 75(F)(ii), I will make additional disclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you cover all of the witnesses that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, by default, the others, there has been no disclosure, so I tried to identify for Your Honour the ones where there has been either complete disclosure, partial disclosure and the ones for MP 005, MP 006, MP 011, MP 013 and MP 015, there has been no disclosure and that is based on, as I say, protective measures granted in other cases. I'm in the process of reviewing those measures and the materials in relation to Rule 75(F)(ii) to see if I can make additional disclosures and I will do so after I've completed my review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Castle and the Chamber will be assisted if this was done speedily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I intend to do so as quickly as I can. I will be unavailable this next week, but I think upon my return I'll be able to finish that review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it should be done within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of today. A full status report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On all of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The only other matter that I have left is the next Status Conference, but before I do that, I should ask Mr. Castle whether he has any matter to raise in relation to the accused, his health or conditions of detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASTLE
utterances.text: We have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, do you have any other matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is one matter, Your Honour. The information we received this week was that Miroslav Deronjic passed away in custody in Sweden. Mr. Deronjic is a listed witness on our 65 ter witness list. He is -- was scheduled to testify viva voce in this case. We will be filing a 92 quater motion then because of the development that we were just informed of, his passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll await that. The next Status Conference has to be held before the 20th of September, and I will set it for Wednesday, the 19th of September. There being no other matters, the hearing is adjourned.
